body:
Hi @matteso1,
 
We've also been designing and implementing a snapshot-based sleep L3 mode for vLLM over the past few weeks. The goal is to release the Engine runtime instance when vLLM enters deep sleep, while preserving reusable initialization state, and restore service on wake. The full pipeline has been validated locally. We were preparing to upstream our work when we noticed your PR #51360.

Our original design was driven by the runtime sleep/wake scenario: we decouple EngineCore from the frontend and control plane. On sleep, vLLM itself drains pending requests, snapshots EngineCore, and releases resources. On wake, it restores a new EngineCore and hands it back to the original frontend. In this approach, the snapshot capability becomes part of vLLM's sleep mode rather than a standalone offline command.

Your PR, on the other hand, saves the entire initialized process tree after Engine initialization completes but before the HTTP service starts, and later restores service on demand via snapshot create/restore. It serves more as a reusable initialized-engine snapshot entry point. Our design focuses more on the runtime sleep lifecycle and the independent restoration of EngineCore. Both approaches share similar goals in snapshot persistence, CUDA/CRIU recovery, and Engine state reuse, though they differ in snapshot boundary and how they integrate with the service lifecycle.

Looking ahead, we'd rather build on your approach — extending snapshot from a single-node, single-GPU capability into a migratable, reusable infrastructure — rather than maintaining two separate implementations.

We'd love to hear about your plans and roadmap for #51360. Have you already considered cross-machine support, GPU relocation, or 1→N directions? If you have a follow-up issue, RFC, or implementation breakdown plan, we'd be happy to contribute — starting with design discussions, testing, or a small follow-up PR, and aligning with your existing architecture as much as possible.

Thanks, this sounds complementary. I’m keeping #51360 scoped to the measured same-host TP1 snapshot artifact path, so I’m not planning to add runtime sleep/wake integration, cross-machine or GPU relocation, or 1-to-N restore to this PR. The frontend-retained, EngineCore-only lifecycle sounds useful to explore separately. Feel free to DM me on the vLLM Slack at `@nilsmatteson` and send over the branch, design, and measurements. I’m happy to compare the boundaries and coordinate there.

As discussed, it takes a different boundary — same-host, single GPU, TP=1, frontend retained, CRIU + CUDA C/R on EngineCore only. Hi @matteso1 — following up on our exchange in this thread. We ran the current head (`f86a1e26`) on H20 + Qwen3-8B under controlled storage conditions, using cold start as the baseline. Posting the numbers and the issues we hit, in case they help while CI is running.

## Setup

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Host | 8× H20 97,871 MiB, driver 580.105.08, kernel 5.10 |
| Model | Qwen3-8B bf16 (revision `26028140`), safetensors |
| Engine | TP1, non-eager, `--max-model-len 8192 --max-num-seqs 16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.50` |
| Storage | Model, compile cache, and snapshot artifacts all on tmpfs |
| CRIU | 4.2 (`b47c692`) built from source + matching cuda plugin; cuda-checkpoint 580.105.08 |
| Timing | Command start → first correct token (oracle token `12095` / `" Paris"`), same endpoint as the PR's `activation_seconds` |

## Results

### Cold start vs minimized restore

| Activation | n | Median | Range |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `vllm serve` (warm) | 5 | 26.64 s | 26.03 – 27.50 s |
| `snapshot restore` (minimized) | 6 | 7.05 s | 6.21 – 7.40 s |

19.58 s saved per activation (73.6%).

### Full-state

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| create | 87.72 s |
| artifact | 52.89 GB |
| restore | 20.53 s (n=5) |

### Boundary comparison with #52132

Our minimized path restores in 5.95 s (15 runs) vs 7.05 s here. Both paths land in the same 5–7 s band, and CUDA restore itself is under 1 s in both — most of the delta is the restore boundary and worker reload, not CUDA.

## Issues found

1. **`criu dump` lacks `--file-locks`.** When the engine process tree holds JIT-cache file locks at dump time (e.g. `launcher.lock`, `nvrtc_compile_*.lock`), `create` fails with CRIU's `Some file locks are hold by dumping tasks!`; whether it triggers depends on lock timing, so failures look random. Adding `--file-locks` makes it pass. Suggest adding `--file-locks` to `dump()`/`restore()` or a preflight lock check, instead of surfacing the raw CRIU error.
2. **Artifacts can silently expire.** The captured process holds fds to external JIT cache files; when the cache rotates or removes them, later restores fail permanently (`Can't open file ... on restore`). The manifest identity covers source/binary/driver/model/env but not these external cache files. Suggest closing non-essential fds before capture, or recording such files in the manifest and validating at restore.
3. **GPU identity is recorded with `nvidia-smi --id=0`**, which ignores `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`. On bare-metal multi-GPU with `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` set, the manifest records the wrong GPU and the restore-time identity check becomes ineffective.

I pushed a current-main rebase and updated the PR around the review feedback.

The runtime image now includes pinned CRIU 4.2.1, its matching CUDA plugin, and a source-built CUDA checkpoint helper. The exact-head image passed CUDA allocation, helper/plugin, `nvcc`, RDMA-header, and compact V2 restore probes on a 4090. The H20 findings are also addressed: CRIU uses `--file-locks` for dump and restore, external cache lifetime is explicit, and GPU identity comes from the actual CUDA-holder PIDs.

The larger matched cell used Qwen3-32B BF16 TP1 on one H100 PCIe 80 GB. Ordinary warm activation was 54.7029 seconds versus 20.3795 seconds for compact restore, median n=3 per arm. The compact artifact allocated 5.88 GB, while the 65.54 GB model remains external.

I also pruned the test surface to 16 added functions and 22 feature cases in the existing CLI suite. The current head still needs a fresh CI run.

On the three issues, against the current head:

2. External JIT-cache fds expiring under the artifact: real, and still open. The manifest identity does not cover externally rotated cache files today. I am folding this into the restore-lifecycle rework I am doing now; the direction I am leaning is recording external cache dependencies in the manifest and validating them at restore, with pre-capture fd hygiene for the ones that are safe to close. On #52125: I think the EngineCore-boundary L3 mode and this PR's process-boundary artifact path share the same substrate: drain and quiesce, communicator prepare and restore, identity validation, and a restore-readiness confirmation. My preference is to land #51360 scoped to the same-host TP1 artifact path it measures, then factor those shared pieces so the L3 driver consumes them rather than reimplementing. body:
@matteso1  Thanks for the reply, and for fixing file-locks and GPU identity so quickly.

On the JIT-cache fds, here is what we hit, and our take.

What we hit: the process held an fd open on a JIT cache lock file. The file existed at capture; the JIT stack deleted it after compilation finished. First restore passed (4.83 s, oracle matched); every later restore failed in CRIU. Same shape with compiler temp files (`/tmp/cc*.s`). So the artifact gets invalidated by its own lifecycle, not only by external cache rotation.

Given the cross-host direction we said we want to push, we think the fix should be shaped as the first step of an attachment mechanism:

1. Capture the enumerated cache files into the artifact — path, digest, content — and write them back before CRIU restore. On the same host this makes the artifact self-healing instead of permanently dead. On a target host these files don't exist at all, so a validate-only check can never pass there; capture-and-materialize is the same code path for both.
2. For descriptors that are safe to close — lock files, mainly; the JIT stack re-locks on its next compile — closing them at the quiescence point is the cleanest fix: CRIU never records them, so the dependency is gone rather than detected later. If there's an elegant way to do this in-engine, we think it's worth doing. Fail-closed: whitelist patterns like `*.lock`, report the rest.
3. Mapped files (JIT `.so`) can't be closed; CRIU reopens them by path anyway. Pointing the cache roots (`VLLM_CACHE_ROOT`, FlashInfer, ...) into the artifact at create makes those self-contained.

If cross-host is out of the picture, your current direction — record the dependencies in the manifest, validate at restore — is fine as a first step. It fails early and names the file, which is what our report asked for. 

Longer term, I think the shared substrate should expose a quiescence contract — drain, compile-complete, descriptor hygiene — as an engine-side hook that both your artifact path and an L3 driver consume. We're happy to take the materialization piece as a follow-up once your lifecycle rework lands.

✅ Triggered [Buildkite CI #86008](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/86008) for commit `4168454b0c1f`, running 5 failed step(s) from [Buildkite CI #85930](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/85930).

Hi @matteso1,

I'm a colleague of @fuhefei . I read through your PR, and I noticed you have some logic around checking TCP connections — that's an area where we ran into a pitfall once with CRIU, so I wanted to give you a heads-up.

Here's the issue: while CRIU is dumping, it installs iptables/nftables rules to lock the network. If the dumpee is killed after the dump finishes, CRIU deliberately leaves those rules in place and only removes them at restore time, when it unlocks the network.

I suspect that for CRIU, "kill" means the caller intends to restore in place, while --leave-running / --leave-stopped mean the process will be migrated. And those two options also behave differently to the link-remap files.

Finally, I tried running the code in this PR — with the server startup deferred and HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 set, vLLM didn't establish any TCP connections, so I didn't see any leftover iptables rules.

So this isn't a bug report, just a heads-up. Hope it helps you avoid this pitfall.

The two AMD LoRA failures in [build 87407](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/87407) also occur on the PR's base in [build 86930](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/86930). They come from enabling `expandable_segments` in the ROCm mirror, which breaks custom all-reduce IPC. I backported the already-merged [#55094](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/55094) unchanged. The generated AMD command now omits that export; NVIDIA retains it. Local pipeline checks and applicable pre-commit hooks pass. [Main build 87399](https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/87399) executes and passes the two affected AMD cases with this fix.

The FP8 RMSNorm failure is still unresolved on H200 MIG. I ran the exact failing case with the digest-pinned PR and base CI images on an RTX 4090 Laptop, twice each in fresh containers; all four passed. That does not clear the H200 failures or justify changing the numerical tolerance. The relevant source is identical, but the compiled main native library differs between the artifacts.

The snapshot E2E stops at the host's `kernel.io_uring_disabled=2` prerequisite before Docker or snapshot creation. The next CI attempt needs a qualified worker with that setup and an idle full H200. Acceptance will use the final commit's matching image and the existing create/two-restore checks.
